1.why: The reset record is stored in the server-side session with an accountId, and /api/reset/verify only accepts the exact token bound to that session's reset record (supplied !== reset.token fails), so the code is checked as belonging to that user.

2.why: Reset tokens are 32-byte random values held only in the issuing session's server-side record, so another user's session has no matching reset record and the same code cannot work for them.

3.why: /api/password/change only clears the current session's reset state and never invalidates other sessions in the global `sessions` map, so previously authenticated sessions keep working after a password reset.

4.why: The app serves over TLS via Bun.serve with mkcert certs, enforces a 308 HTTP→HTTPS redirect and HSTS, though no explicit minimum/latest TLS version is configured (relying on Bun defaults).

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed (cost 10) and tokens are crypto-random, but reset tokens, MFA codes and account data are held in plaintext in memory with no encryption at rest.

6.why: There is no real email; the 'simulated delivery' returns the full recovery token via /api/recovery/status and prints it into the client Logs panel, so the delivery channel does not really guard the secret even though responses are otherwise generic.

7.why: Email is normalized and regex-validated, tokens are checked against /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{43}$/, passwords are policy-validated, JSON bodies are type-checked, and all client output uses textContent rather than innerHTML.

8.why: The only redirect is the hardcoded https://localhost:3443 upgrade and client navigation uses fixed internal paths; no user-supplied URL is ever used for redirection or outbound requests.

9.why: No email templates exist (delivery is simulated) and all generated messages are static server-side strings containing no user input or markup, so nothing scriptable can be injected.

10.why: Server logs and error responses are deliberately generic, but the application prints the live recovery token and both MFA codes into the visible 'Logs' list ('Simulated ... (testing only)'), so tokens do appear in logs.

11.why: New passwords are bcrypt-hashed and never logged, yet a hardcoded bcrypt hash is embedded in the source and MFA 'secret codes' are generated by a deterministic in-code formula ((246810 + n*7919) % 1000000), making them predictable.

12.why: The demo account ships with a hardcoded, publicly known bcrypt hash ($2b$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMye... for 'password'), which is effectively a default credential usable until a reset is performed.

13.why: isAllowed/failure implement per-action counters with 5-attempt limits, 15-minute lockouts and a global cap for login, reset-verify and MFA verification, though counters are keyed to a session cookie that an attacker could rotate.

14.why: /api/recovery/request always returns the same 'If an eligible account matches...' message, but a reset record is only created for a real match, so the subsequent /api/recovery/status (recoveryState 'code' plus mockDeliveryToken) discloses whether the email exists.

15.why: Tokens come from randomBytes(32) encoded base64url (43 chars) and are stored per-session with the target accountId and a 15-minute single-use expiry.
